High intra-rater reliability is essential in research studies where measurements are taken by a single observer, as it ensures that the results are accurate and not influenced by rater variability. For instance, in a clinical trial, if a researcher is assessing the efficacy of a new treatment using a subjective outcome measure, intra-rater reliability is crucial to ensure that any observed changes are due to the treatment and not the rater's inconsistency. ### Importance in Research Studies and Applications Intra-rater reliability is vital in various research studies and applications, including: * Clinical trials: To ensure that outcome measures are assessed consistently and accurately. Methods for Assessing Intra-Rater Reliability Several statistical measures and study design considerations can be used to assess intra-rater reliability. ### Statistical Measures Some common statistical measures used to assess intra-rater reliability include: * **Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC)**: The ICC is a widely used measure of intra-rater reliability that assesses the consistency of measurements taken by a single rater. It is used to assess the limits of agreement between two measurements and can be used to evaluate intra-rater reliability. Intra-rater reliability is a crucial aspect of biostatistics that ensures the accuracy and consistency of measurements taken by a single rater or observer. Intra-rater reliability refers to the degree of consistency with which a single rater or observer measures a particular variable or outcome. Intra-rater reliability is essential in research studies where measurements are taken by a single observer, as it ensures that the results are accurate and not influenced by rater variability. Intra-rater reliability can be assessed using statistical measures such as the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), kappa coefficient, and Bland-Altman plot. Some common challenges and pitfalls that can affect intra-rater reliability include rater bias, lack of training, measurement variability, and fatigue or observer drift.

results.title: Assessment of the Human Factors Analysis and Classification System (HFACS): Intra-rater and Inter-rater Reliability
results.content:
Title: Assessment of the Human Factors Analysis and Classification System (HFACS): Intra-rater and Inter-rater Reliability
# Assessment of the Human Factors Analysis and Classification System (HFACS): Intra-rater and Inter-rater Reliability. One of the most important safety taxonomies is the Human Factors Analysis and Classification System (HFACS) (Harris & Li, 2011), a comprehensive accident investigation and analysis tool which focuses not only on the act of the individual preceding the accident but on other contributing factors in the system (environmental, supervisory, and organizational). The systems approach models, which include a combination effect of many factors including human error contribution to accidents, include the SHEL Model (Edwards, 1988; in Wiegmann & Shappell, 2003), the Swiss-cheese model (SCM) (Reason, 1990; 2008), the wheel of misfortune (O'hare, 2000), the incident cause analysis method (ICAM) (Gibb, Hayward, & Lowe, 2001), and the human factors analysis and classification system (HFACS) (Wiegmann & Shappell, 1997; 2001a). The Human Factors Analysis and Classification System (HFACS) is a human error taxonomy developed to provide a comprehensive framework to identify and classify causal factors of incidents/accidents; then based on these data, safety interventions can be developed and subsequently, their effectiveness evaluated (Shappel & Wiegmann, 2000). For example, the analysis of the majority of industrial accidents using HFACS, whether national or international, revealed that at the level of unsafe acts of operators, the most prevalent category was skill-based errors, including memory lapse, distraction, and poor technique (e.g., aviation: Boquet, Detwiler, Hackworth, Holomb, & Pfleiderer, 2007; Li, Harris, & Yu, 2008; S. However, the remaining 5 categories – Skill Based Error, Decision Error, Inadequate Supervision, Planned Inappropriate Operations and Supervisory Violation – exhibited unacceptable intra-rater reliability levels, indicating that the coders were inconsistent in their responses of classifying the causal factors corresponding to these categories. Furthermore, research has found that for taxonomies including a hierarchy of exhaustive, mutually exclusive categories, like HFACS, coder agreements are expected to vary according to specific training requirements (Annett & Duncan, 1967), affecting both the inter-rater and intra-rater reliability levels. Future studies on the reliability of HFACS should be designed to include coders coding actual causal factors from incident/accident reports in addition to the other factors 131. results.title: Journal of Rehabilitation Medicine - Inter- and intra-rater variability of testing velocity when assessing lower limb spasticity - HTML
results.content: ***Objective:* To establish the variability of fast testing velocity and joint range of motion and position when assessing lower-limb spasticity in individuals following neurological injury.**. ***Methods:* The Modified Tardieu scale (MTS) was completed on the quadriceps, hamstrings (2 positions), gastrocnemius and soleus for each participant’s more affected lower limb by 3 assessors. ***Results:* Variability of peak testing velocity was greater at the ankle joint compared with the knee joint. The greatest MAD for V3 (fast) inter-rater testing velocity was 119°/s in the soleus, representing 29.4% of the mean variable value, and least for the quadriceps (64.3°/s; 18.5%). ***Conclusion:* There was a large degree of inter- and intra-rater variability in V3 testing velocity when using the MTS to assess lower limb spasticity. The secondary aim was to establish the inter- and intra-rater variability of the joint start angles, end angles and total range of motion (ROM) at V1 (slow) and V3, as well as the V1 peak testing velocity when assessing for lower limb spasticity using the MTS.
